lesson.title: The Storytelling Past
lesson.subtitle: The imparfait camera lens: c'était, j'avais, j'habitais, je voulais — ongoing background vs. completed event

hook.title: The Movie Camera vs. the Snapshot
hook.content: When you tell a story about the past, your mind uses two different cameras. One camera takes a sharp snapshot of a single completed action ('Yesterday I bought a ticket, I took the train') — that is the passé composé (j'ai pris). The second camera pans across the ongoing background scene, how things used to be, or what was happening ('It was raining, I lived in Lyon, I had a small apartment, I wanted to travel') — that is l'imparfait ('the imperfect / unfinished past')!

footnotes.title: Why every single verb in the imparfait uses the exact same endings
footnotes.content: Take the nous form of ANY verb in the present (nous avons → av-, nous habitons → habit-, nous voulons → voul-) and add -ais, -ais, -ait (/ɛ/)! Only être has a special stem (ét- → c'était 'it was').

pattern.title: The Universal /ɛ/ Sound of -ais and -ait
pattern.content: Listen to how simple the singular imparfait is: j'avais ('I had'), tu avais ('you had'), il/elle avait ('he/she had') ALL end in the exact same open /ɛ/ sound! Likewise: j'habitais ('I lived / used to live'), je voulais ('I wanted'), and the superstar pointer c'était ('it was'). Whenever you combine both pasts in one sentence, the imparfait sets the ongoing stage (Quand j'habitais à Paris...) and the passé composé drops the sudden event (...j'ai rencontré Marie)!
pattern.linguist_note: Latin imperfect -ēbam/-ēbat evolved regularly into Old French -eie/-eit and modern French -ais/-ait /ɛ/.
pattern.trap_note: The shortcut your mind will offer: using C'est été or Il a été for 'It was good'. When describing how something was in the past, ALWAYS reach for C'était: C'était très bon!

exercises.prompt: Match each imparfait form with its ongoing past meaning:
exercises.target_answer: it was / that was, I had / used to have, I lived / was living, I wanted / was wanting, he / it was
exercises.meaning: c'était (from c'est), j'avais (from j'ai), j'habitais (from j'habite), je voulais (from je veux), il était (from il est)
exercises.explanation: Notice how -ais and -ait are pronounced identically (/ɛ/).

exercises.prompt: You want to say 'The coffee was very good' (describing its state/quality in the past). Which tense fits?
options: Le café a été très bon
exercises.explanation: Background descriptions and states in the past always take the imparfait (était).

exercises.prompt: Which English sentences accurately express 'J'habitais à Lyon'?
exercises.meaning: I lived / used to live / was living in Lyon
renderings: I used to live in Lyon
traps: I have just moved to Lyon today
I am going to live in Lyon
exercises.target_answer: I used to live in Lyon
exercises.explanation: The French imparfait covers English 'used to [verb]', 'was [verb]-ing', and ongoing past 'lived'.

exercises.idea: it was very good and I wanted to stay
cues: It was very good → C'était très bon + and I wanted to stay → et je voulais rester
idea_parts: ongoing desire → et je voulais rester
exercises.target_answer: C'était très bon et je voulais rester
exercises.meaning: It was very good and I wanted to stay
exercises.explanation: Both c'était and je voulais paint ongoing past states, so both use the imparfait.

diagnosis.cue: Use C'était ('it was') and je voulais ('I wanted').

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the whole sentence.
exercises.spoken: Quand j'habitais à Paris, j'avais un vélo
exercises.target_answer: Quand j'habitais à Paris, j'avais un vélo
exercises.meaning: When I lived in Paris, I had a bike
cues: When I lived in Paris: Quand j'habitais à Paris
I had a bike: j'avais un vélo
exercises.explanation: Two ongoing past states side by side: habitais and avais.
exercises.affirmation: You caught both -ais endings on habitais and avais.

summary.outcome: Use the imparfait (-ais/-ait) for past descriptions, habits, and background scenes, and contrast it with the passé composé.

use_example.german: C'était magnifique quand nous habitions là.
use_example.english: It was wonderful when we used to live there.

summary.takeaway: Passé composé is the event dot; imparfait (-ais/-ait) is the background canvas — and c'était is its king.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next on Le Pont ([1901] Was & Was-Ing): see how The Storytelling Past leads directly into Was & Was-Ing.

twist.prompt: Ungraded — combine both pasts: 'I wanted to come, but I did not have the time' (use mais je n'avais pas le temps):
twist.target_answer: Je voulais venir, mais je n'avais pas le temps
twist.explanation: Ongoing past desire (je voulais) + ongoing past lack of time (je n'avais pas le temps).

foreshadow.line: Having mastered The Storytelling Past, look ahead to Topic 20 (depuis & the Perfect Split), where this machinery expands into the next dimension of French thought.

payoff.text: The foundation from Topic 18 (Motion Takes être) now pays off directly inside The Storytelling Past: every sentence here builds on that earlier step.

était.etymology_derivation: être's imparfait — the background tense, the was of a story already in motion.

avais.english_meaning: had, used to have (j'avais / tu avais)
avais.context_translation: I used to have a small car.
avais.etymology_derivation: Imparfait paints the ongoing background setting.

habitais.etymology_derivation: Take the nous stem (habit-) and add -ais, -ais, -ait, -ions, -iez, -aient.

voulais.context_translation: I wanted to talk to you.
voulais.etymology_derivation: Used for ongoing past desires or polite softening ('I was wanting to ask...').

habiter.context_translation: I've lived here for three years.
habiter.etymology_derivation: habitāre 'to dwell often' — a habitat is where a thing dwells; habits are where you dwell repeatedly. With depuis, it stays present tense.

utiliser.context_translation: I used to ride my bike.

cest.english_meaning: it is; this is; that is
cest.etymology_derivation: ce ('that') + est — the elision French performs constantly: a vowel before a vowel loses its tail.

avoir.etymology_derivation: Latin habēre = have. The H dropped and stayed dropped — French never pronounces its Latin H.

vouloir.etymology_derivation: Latin volō 'I want' → vouloir. A volunteer is the one who wants to do — the want-root English kept in voluntary, benevolent.
